read.sections.0.heading.back: People everywhere tell stories about beginnings
read.sections.0.heading.source: People everywhere tell accounts of beginnings

read.sections.0.text.note: Translator: Faith wording to check with members of each faith: 'Tuhan mencipta langit dan bumi' (Islam, Christianity, Judaism), the Hindu cycle of time, and 'makhluk nenek moyang' for Aboriginal ancestral beings. 'Makhluk' may sound too much like 'creature'. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. Faith wording needs checking by members of each faith: 'Tuhan mencipta langit dan bumi', the Hindu cycle of time, and 'makhluk nenek moyang', where 'makhluk' may sound like 'creature'. 'Orang Asli Australia' follows the brief, but readers may link it to Malaysian Orang Asli. 'Mewariskan kisah ... melalui cerita dan lagu' repeats itself a little. A reviewer may want a better word here.
read.sections.0.text.back: People all over the world have asked where the world came from. Many communities have origin stories. These stories tell how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as one great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is created, ends and then begins again. Many Aboriginal Australians tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, water and animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass down their own stories through stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin story, such as the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Stories like these carry the beliefs and values of a group.
read.sections.0.text.source: People all over the world have asked where the world came from. Many communities have an origin account. It tells how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as a great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is made, ends and then begins again. Many Aboriginal peoples of Australia tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, the water and the animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass on their own accounts in stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, like the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Accounts like these carry a group's beliefs and values.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Translator: 'Makhluk dari zaman dahulu' for Aboriginal ancestral beings: check with someone who knows Aboriginal Australian traditions that this sounds respectful. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. Check that 'makhluk dari zaman dahulu' sounds respectful for Aboriginal traditions. The simpler English also says 'beings from long ago', so no meaning was lost. 'Orang Asli' may make readers think of Malaysian Orang Asli.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: People all over the world ask how everything began. Many groups have origin stories. These stories tell how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God created the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and begins again. This happens over and over. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of beings from ancient times. These beings shaped the land and animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific have their own stories. Our invented town, Tallgrass Valley, also has its own story. These stories carry beliefs and values.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: People all over the world ask how it all began. Many groups have an origin account. It tells how things began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God made the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and starts again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of beings from long ago. These beings made the land and the animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific have their own accounts. Our made-up town, Tallgrass Valley, has one too. These accounts hold beliefs and values.

read.sections.1.text.back: Each kind of explanation can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in the natural world. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has kept expanding since then. Religious explanations and cultural explanations often answer other questions. Why does this world exist? What matters most? How should people treat one another? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an explanation, when and why. Look again at the three questions about beginnings. Each one needs a different kind of answer.
read.sections.1.text.source: Each kind of account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been growing ever since. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer other questions. Why is there a world? What matters most? How should people treat each other? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an account, when, and why. Look again at the three questions about beginnings. Each one needs a different kind of answer.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Each explanation can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in the natural world. They use evidence that can be seen and tested. Historians ask who told an explanation, and why. Each question needs its own kind of answer.

read.sections.2.heading.back: We learn about explanations with respect
read.sections.2.heading.source: We learn about accounts with respect

read.sections.2.text.note: Translator: 'Menyusun kedudukan' is used for 'rank'. Check that young readers will understand it. Back-translation check: 'Menyusun kedudukannya' is used for 'rank them'. It is correct but wordy for children. A native reviewer may prefer a simpler phrase, and should change it the same way in read.checks.1.options.0.feedback, read.checks.1.options.1.feedback and sensitiveNotes.1.
read.sections.2.text.back: In this lesson, we learn about these explanations, but we do not judge them or arrange their rankings. Respect means describing each explanation carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe ..." for religious explanations and "Scientists explain ..." for scientific explanations. Many people hold religious explanations and scientific explanations at the same time, and many scientists are also religious people. No one has to share what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an explanation, check a trusted source or ask a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.source: In this lesson, we learn about accounts, but we do not judge them or rank them. Respect means describing each account carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe ..." for a faith account and "Scientists explain ..." for a science account. Many people hold both a faith account and a science account, and many scientists are also people of faith. Nobody has to share what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an account, check a trusted source or ask a teacher.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Here, we learn about explanations. We do not judge them. We do not say one explanation is best. Respect means we describe each explanation carefully. We never laugh at it. Say "Many people believe" for religion. Say "Scientists explain" for science. Many people accept both kinds of explanation. You do not have to share your own beliefs.

write.example.back: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people can use evidence measured by scientists. For example, they study light from distant stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer it, people can listen to the elders. They can think about the promise to share the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One question asks how something happens in the natural world. The other asks what is important to a group of people.
write.example.source: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people could use evidence that scientists measure. For example, they study light from faraway stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer it, people could listen to the elders. They could think about the promise to share the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One asks how something happened in nature. The other asks what matters to a group of people.

The English says 'groups of stars', so 'kumpulan bintang' is correct.
watch.summary.back: This video gives a scientific explanation of how the universe began. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first, it was very small and very hot. Since then, it has become bigger and colder. Scientists use evidence they can measure. For example, they see that distant groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still expanding. They also found faint light left over from when the universe was still very young. Scientific explanations like this answer questions about how things happen in the natural world. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need a different kind of answer. Many people value scientific explanations and also religious explanations.
watch.summary.source: This video gives a science account of how the universe began. Scientists explain that it began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first, it was very small and very hot. Since then, it has grown bigger and cooler. Scientists use evidence they can measure. For example, they see that faraway groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still growing. They also find a faint glow left over from when the universe was very young. A science account like this answers questions about how things happen in nature. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need other kinds of answers. Many people value both a science account and a faith account.
